newsitem.title: UK: Quasars are the final frontier, astronomers say.
newsitem.headline: Quasars are the final frontier, astronomers say.

text.p: Quasars, distant and mysterious objects that have intrigued astronomers for 30 years, can be used to calculate the age of the earliest galaxies and thus of the universe, European astronomers said on Wednesday.
They said they had finally solved the puzzle of whether the most distant quasars really are the most distant -- or whether there are some more hiding behind dust.
There aren't, is the answer they give in a report in the scientific journal Nature said.
"This means we can pinpoint the beginning phase of the universe as we know it," Jasper Wall, a cosmologist at Cambridge University who worked on the study, said.
Quasars are extremely bright but extremely distant. They are believed to be at the heart of young galaxies, marking the explosive deaths of stars as they are sucked into black holes.

Scientists thought they probably were the most distant objects seen, which, because the universe is expanding, would make them the oldest. But there was the possibility that more were obscured behind cosmic dust.
Wall and colleagues at the European Southern Observatory in Garching bei Munchen in Germany looked at radio signals from quasars. Radio signals would not be affected by dust.
"They do exactly the same thing," Wall said, which meant that the visible quasars were indeed the most distant.

Wall's group said this, in turn, meant they could be used to measure the age of galaxy formation, and thus of the universe. Their measurements confirm that galaxies first started forming when the universe was about one-tenth of its present age.
Astronomers cannot put an exact fix on how many years that is because they do not know how fast the universe is expanding. It could be anywhere between nine and 17 billion years old.
